title: Chart Spin — the same numbers, both ways
subtitle: One query, one dataset, two opposite arguments — and every number on both charts is correct

source.publisher: Same DOHMH data as the Inspections tab — that is the point
source.note: Both charts below are produced by one script in one run from one API call. No data was added, removed, or altered between them. Everything that differs is a display choice.

grain.row_is: one violation citation, rated per inspection

counts.label: levers that differ between the two

grain.note: The honest chart's window was fixed by the question before looking. The spun chart's window was chosen by searching all 15 possible 12-month starts for the one that maximized Brooklyn's slope — a choice that leaves no visual trace whatsoever.

charts.title: The honest render
charts.insight: Brooklyn's violations-per-inspection went 3.67 → 3.67 over the last twelve complete months. Flat. Its annualized drift (+0.19/yr) ranks third behind the Bronx (+0.32) and Manhattan (+0.23), and all five boroughs sit inside a narrow band.
charts.form: Multi-line, zero baseline, one accented series
charts.form_why: The claim under test was about change over time across groups, so time goes on x and every borough shares one y-scale. Graying four series and accenting one is emphasis — it directs attention without altering what any line shows.
charts.method: y-axis from zero so visible change equals real change. Window = last 12 complete calendar months, fixed by the question before any data was seen. No smoothing. Identical treatment for every line. Partial current month excluded.
charts.caution: This chart's headline is that a premise handed to us — 'Brooklyn is steadily rising while others stay flat' — turned out to be false. The honest render could not make that claim, so it doesn't.

charts.title: The spun render — same data, four levers moved
charts.insight: 'BROOKLYN VIOLATIONS SURGE 12 MONTHS RUNNING.' Manufactured from a 14% wobble in a dataset where the honest answer was +0.00. Nothing here is fabricated; every plotted value is real.
charts.form_why: Identical form, opposite conclusion — which is the whole demonstration. Spin does not require a different chart type or a false number. It requires four defensible-sounding choices.
charts.method: 1) Window cherry-picked as the max-slope option out of 15 candidates, starting at Brooklyn's trough. 2) y-axis zoomed to Brooklyn's own range, so a 14% change fills 100% of panel height — hiding behind the true rule that line charts need not start at zero. 3) Tall-narrow aspect ratio amplifies any slope; nobody audits aspect ratio. 4) Three-month smoothing applied to Brooklyn ONLY (disclosed at 5.5pt), so its cleaned line reads as signal while the raw grays read as noise.
charts.caution: Every individual choice here has a legitimate use, and each could be defended in a meeting by citing a real principle. That is what makes this the realistic failure mode — far more common than fabricated data, and much harder to catch.

charts.title: Side by side — every axis labeled, and the right panel still lies
charts.insight: Both panels carry full axis labels and their own disclosure line. The deception survives anyway, because it lives in the frame rather than in anything a label can name.
charts.form_why: Equal panels isolate the levers under study. An earlier version drew the spun panel narrower — preserving the aspect trick — which confounded 'the y-axis is zoomed' with 'the panel is squished' and made the comparison itself guilty of the thing it teaches.
charts.method: Left and right render from the same array of numbers in the same script execution. The only differences are y-range, window, and which series got smoothed.
charts.caution: 'The axes are labeled, just read them' is the standard defense of a spun chart. This image is the counterexample. Window, y-range, aspect ratio and asymmetric smoothing have no axis labels — so a reader who checks only the labels has audited nothing.

cannot_answer: Whether any particular published chart was spun deliberately. These four levers are also the everyday choices of honest charting; intent is not visible in the output, which is precisely why disclosure matters more than motive.
Whether a chart is trustworthy from the chart alone. Two of these levers — the window search and the asymmetric smoothing — leave no visual trace at all. You need the method, not just the image.

How to make an unambiguously neutral chart, because there isn't one. Every chart chooses a window, a baseline, an aspect ratio, a smoothing policy, a color assignment and a caption. The honest ones disclose those choices; they do not avoid making them.
reproduce: python3 data/socrata/viz_borough_trend.py — writes honest.png, misleading.png and comparison.png in a single run
